item.title: Think Halloween is scary? This scorched alien world is a real-life cosmic horror story
item.description: null Earth would be terrifying if we celebrated Halloween every 11 hours, a possibility on a super-Earth investigated by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). That is, if this extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, wasn't so hellishly hot that no life could survive on its surface. The exoplanet in question is the rocky lava planet TOI-561 b, located around 280 light-years away, which was discovered by NASA's exoplanet-hunting spacecraft TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) in 2020. The planet is located so close to its star, TOI-561, that not only does it complete an orbit every 11 hours, but its surface temperatures reach in excess of 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit (1,800 degrees Celsius). That is so hot that astronomers once believed that TOI-561 b couldn't possibly possess an atmosphere. With 37 hours of JWST observations covering nearly four full orbits of TOI-561, scientists have now found this horrific planet is buried in a reflective layer of vaporized silicate mineral clouds, the same family of compounds that make up quartz and sand. "We measured how the planet's brightness and heat changed throughout its orbit," team member Lisa Dang of the University of Waterloo said in a statement. "This technique, known as a phase curve, revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side. Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere." The hemispheres of lava super-Earth are day and night The proximity of TOI-561 b to its star has another consequence. The planet is tidally locked, meaning it doesn't turn like Earth . Thus, TOI-561 b has one blisteringly hot "dayside" permanently facing its star, and a cooler "nightside" facing out into space in perpetuity. Dang and colleagues investigated the fact that the bare rock of the dayside seemed to be cooler than should be expected. They theorized that missing heat could be carried around to the night side or the heat may be reflected away before TOI-561 b can absorb it. By using the JWST to observe full orbits of TOI-561 b, the team was able to observe the planet's nightside for the first time. They found it isn't warm enough to account for all the heat missing from the dayside. That means TOI-561 b must reflect roughly three-quarters of the starlight that hits it. That is comparable to the most reflective planet in the solar system, Venus , which reflects around 75% of incident sunlight compared to the 30% reflected by Earth. The team determined that this high reflectivity is the result of clouds of silicate minerals, including silicon dioxide and magnesium silicate, forming on the planet's dayside and acting like sunscreen. These clouds could also help TOI-561 b hang on to an atmosphere. A diagram shows that TOI-561 b and its two exoplanet siblings would fit well within the orbit of Mercury around the sun (Image credit: NASA) Of course, the team can't yet be sure what this atmosphere

That is, if this extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, wasn't so hellishly hot that no life could survive on its surface. That is so hot that astronomers once believed that TOI-561 b couldn't possibly possess an atmosphere. Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere." The hemispheres of lava super-Earth are day and night The proximity of TOI-561 b to its star has another consequence. Thus, TOI-561 b has one blisteringly hot "dayside" permanently facing its star, and a cooler "nightside" facing out into space in perpetuity. The team determined that this high reflectivity is the result of clouds of silicate minerals, including silicon dioxide and magnesium silicate, forming on the planet's dayside and acting like sunscreen. These clouds could also help TOI-561 b hang on to an atmosphere. A diagram shows that TOI-561 b and its two exoplanet siblings would fit well within the orbit of Mercury around the sun (Image credit: NASA) Of course, the team can't yet be sure what this atmosphere is composed of. It could be a dense carbon dioxide fog like that seen on Venus, or it could be a blanket of sulfur dioxide like that of the most volcanic body in the solar system, Jupiter's moon Io . That would be the case if, like on Io, volcanic activity is replenishing the atmosphere of TOI-561 b. "The next big question we will seek to answer is whether TOI-561 b's atmosphere resembles Venus or an extreme version of Io," Dang said. "Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years." The team's research was published in The Astronomical Journal.

item.title: Scientists confirm fruit and vegetable skin really is good for you
item.description: Fruit and vegetable skin is often rich in fibre Ekaterina Vasileva-Bagler/Getty Images Some people are convinced that fruit and vegetable skin is particularly nutritious, and now scientists have confirmed the idea. They have discovered that these parts of fruits and vegetables often contain far more fibre than the flesh we normally consume. The finding suggests cooks are unwittingly discarding fibre-rich food by chucking out the seeds, skins and stems of fruits and vegetables when preparing a meal. Home cooks and caterers should adopt “root to tip” eating and start cooking with squash peel, watermelon rind and pepper stalks to improve the public’s intake of dietary fibre, the team says. Advertisement Read more Our food system is vulnerable to El Niño, warns UK climate minister “We’ve really got to shift our purchasing habits to buy whole fruits and vegetables, and then use all of the fruits and vegetables in dishes,” says Rachel Gibson at King’s College London. Gibson and her colleagues tested the fibre content of 12 fruits and vegetables, including butternut squash, kiwi fruit, watermelon, broccoli and bell pepper. The team measured the fibre content both in the parts typically consumed and the parts that usually go to waste. They found that, in 10 of the 12 produce types, the normally wasted components contain more fibre than the commonly consumed parts. Butternut squash seeds and skin, for example, contained 9.25 grams of fibre per 100 grams, compared with 2 g of fibre per 100 g of squash flesh. Meanwhile, the skin and core of a pineapple core contains 450 per cent more fibre than the flesh. These skin and core components are often tough to chew, but the researchers say they can be blended, grated or roasted to make them more palatable. Free newsletter Sign up to The Weekly Sign up to newsletter Just 4 per cent of British adults meet the recommended minimum daily intake of 30 g of dietary fibre, with the average adult consuming around half that per day. Gibson suggests caterers could use the findings to design fibre-rich meals using more produce that would otherwise go to waste. This could reduce food waste and cut costs for commercial kitchens, as well as increasing dietary fibre intake, she says. King’s College London’s canteen piloted a “root to tip” menu in May 2025. Meals included a West African peanut stew made with all of a butternut squash, kale stalks and leek tops, and a watermelon salad featuring pickled watermelon rind. Simple menu tweak can nudge people into choosing climate-friendly food Rejigging the meal choices on offer in a canteen can prompt people to make healthier, climate-friendlier decisions Eating a larger proportion of harvested fruit and vegetables will also improve the resilience of the food system in the face of climate shocks , says Gibson. “Everything we pull out of the ground that we can eat, we should be eating.” Christian Reynolds at City St George’s University of London says the research is an “exciting invest

These skin and core components are often tough to chew, but the researchers say they can be blended, grated or roasted to make them more palatable. Free newsletter Sign up to The Weekly Sign up to newsletter Just 4 per cent of British adults meet the recommended minimum daily intake of 30 g of dietary fibre, with the average adult consuming around half that per day. Gibson suggests caterers could use the findings to design fibre-rich meals using more produce that would otherwise go to waste. This could reduce food waste and cut costs for commercial kitchens, as well as increasing dietary fibre intake, she says. King’s College London’s canteen piloted a “root to tip” menu in May 2025. Meals included a West African peanut stew made with all of a butternut squash, kale stalks and leek tops, and a watermelon salad featuring pickled watermelon rind. Simple menu tweak can nudge people into choosing climate-friendly food Rejigging the meal choices on offer in a canteen can prompt people to make healthier, climate-friendlier decisions Eating a larger proportion of harvested fruit and vegetables will also improve the resilience of the food system in the face of climate shocks , says Gibson. “Everything we pull out of the ground that we can eat, we should be eating.” Christian Reynolds at City St George’s University of London says the research is an “exciting investigation”. But he points out that the most carbon-intensive food waste is meat and dairy products. Reducing fruit and vegetable waste is therefore “part of the solution, but it’s not the only thing we need to do”, he says. Journal Reference: International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition DOI: 10.1080/09637486.2026.2734852

item.title: In Dark Eden, I imagined how life might exist on a sunless planet
item.description: Eden, the planet in Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden, drifts outside the Milky Way McCarthy's PhotoWorks/Shutterstock I came up with the idea of the planet Eden in 1992 for a short story called The Circle of Stones . At that time, I had no idea that there really were such things as planets without suns, but it seemed likely to me. It also seemed possible to me that life might arise on such a planet, since, even here on Earth, whole ecologies thrive without sunlight around thermal vents in the deep ocean. Life on Earth may have even have begun in such places. Quite often, if something seems likely, it does indeed happen. (In another book , I predicted that a US president would one day seek to take over Greenland and Canada.) Having written that story, I learned that free-floating planets did indeed exist. Being dark, they’re hard to spot, but a number have been detected using gravitational lensing . And I gather it’s not particularly controversial to think that some of them might support life (though not quite in the form that I chose to imagine it – but I’ll come to that). When creating a world for a story, I don’t usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent. I didn’t build Eden by doing a lot of research, but I did put a lot of thought into how it might all work. This wasn’t so I could put it all in the book – no one in Eden knows this stuff and the story is told entirely by its characters! – but so that I had something to guide my imagination and make my invented world feel coherent. Advertisement Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter My idea was that Eden had once been covered in ice, but its hot core meant there was liquid water below the ice in which life could come into existence. One particular kind of life form appeared, somewhat resembling tree roots, that was able to obtain additional energy by pushing deep down into hot rocks, pumping its sap through them to heat it, and then pumping it back up again, like a geothermal power station. One of the ways these organisms used this heat was to push upwards into the planet’s shell of ice, melting parts of it, feeding on the nutrients it contained, and creating more living space – and they carried on doing so until much of the surface of Eden was ice-free, and had an atmosphere that would turn out to be breathable by humans. Millions of years later, this thawed-out surface, now populated by a multitude of different life forms, became the stage on which my drama could unfold: first that early story, then another story and then the novel Dark Eden and its two sequels. item.dc:creator: Chris Beckett
item.content:encoded: Eden, the planet in Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden, drifts outside the Milky Way McCarthy's PhotoWorks/Shutterstock I came up with the idea of the planet Eden in 1992 for a short story called The Circle of Stones . At that time, I had no idea that there really were such things as planets without suns, but it seemed likely to me. It also seemed possible to me that life might arise on such a planet, since, even here on Earth, whole ecologies thrive without sunlight around thermal vents in the deep ocean. Life on Earth may have even have begun in such places. Quite often, if something seems likely, it does indeed happen. (In another book , I predicted that a US president would one day seek to take over Greenland and Canada.) Having written that story, I learned that free-floating planets did indeed exist. Being dark, they’re hard to spot, but a number have been detected using gravitational lensing . And I gather it’s not particularly controversial to think that some of them might support life (though not quite in the form that I chose to imagine it – but I’ll come to that). When creating a world for a story, I don’t usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent. I didn’t build Eden by doing a lot of research, but I did put a lot of thought into how it might all work. This wasn’t so I could put it all in the book – no one in Eden knows this stuff and the story is told entirely by its characters! – but so that I had something to guide my imagination and make my invented world feel coherent. Advertisement Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter My idea was that Eden had once been covered in ice, but its hot core meant there was liquid water below the ice in which life could come into existence. One particular kind of life form appeared, somewhat resembling tree roots, that was able to obtain additional energy by pushing deep down into hot rocks, pumping its sap through them to heat it, and then pumping it back up again, like a geothermal power station. One of the ways these organisms used this heat was to push upwards into the planet’s shell of ice, melting parts of it, feeding on the nutrients it contained, and creating more living space – and they carried on doing so until much of the surface of Eden was ice-free, and had an atmosphere that would turn out to be breathable by humans. Millions of years later, this thawed-out surface, now populated by a multitude of different life forms, became the stage on which my drama could unfold: first that early story, then another story and then the novel Dark Eden and its two sequels. In Dark Eden , a tiny community of humans, descended from stranded visitors from Earth, eke out a living using tools made of stone and wood, and try to make sense of their life as exiles from a sunlit world that lives on in folk memory, but which they can only very shakily imagine. (In the biblical story of Eden, humans are exiled from Eden – my Eden is the place of exile.) Their stories tell them that Earth people could fly through the air, that there was a thing there called leckytrickity, that Earth animals had eyes that you could look into and see their minds looking back out at you, not like the flat, blank eyes of Eden creatures. Read more Our writers pick their favourite science fiction books of all time On the surface of Eden, those root-like life forms put up structures that Eden’s humans call “trees”. A whole ecosystem has evolved around them, including “starflowers” that parasitise their roots. (These, as it happens, turn out to be a rich source of Vitamin D. Phew! What a stroke of luck!) And there are many animals – or quote-unquote “animals”, strictly speaking, since they’re not related to the animal kingdom of Earth. There’s no sunlight in Eden (and therefore no alternation of day and night) but, like organisms that live in the ocean depths of Earth, Eden’s life has developed bioluminescence. The “trees” have luminous “lanternflowers”; the starflowers glitter. Imagine a leafless forest on a moonless night, lit by thousands of Chinese lanterns. Then add in twinkling fairy lights at ground level. With your eyes half-closed, the forests of Eden would look something like that. Just as life on Earth depends on plants that turn sunlight into chemical energy, so the life of Eden depends on geothermal trees. They bring heat to the surface to power their metabolisms, they keep the air warm and, if you live on Eden, the steady “ Hmmmph hmmmph hmmmph ” of their constant pumping is the background of your waking and sleeping life, merging in the distance to a steady hum. All the trees are hot, and some of them are so hot that you’d burn yourself if you touched their trunks. If you cut down a tree, you have to watch out for the spurt of scalding liquid that bursts out. When I read stories set on alien planets, I’m sometimes disappointed in the “animals” (I’ll drop the inverted commas now). Writers often seem to dream up a motley collection of bizarre creatures without much regard for how they might actually survive or how they are related to one another. I tried to design my animals on evolutionary principles, giving thought to how they were adapted to their environment, the role they played in the ecosystem and how they might plausibly have evolved. Animals on Earth fall into a large but finite number of basic body plans. For example, monkeys, cows, crocodiles and seagulls all have four limbs and, though some descendants of quadrupeds have lost their limbs (snakes, whales), there are no examples of quadrupeds developing extra ones. In the same way, large animals on Eden all have a six-limbed body plan. There are other animals that don’t conform to this, just as there are arthropods, et cetera on Earth, but the large animals are all based on this six-limbed pattern. The 12 best science fiction books of 2025 From drowned worlds to virtual utopias via deep space, wild ideas abound in Emily H. Wilson’s picks for her favourite sci-fi reads of the year I’ve already mentioned how different Eden eyes are from the eyes of terrestrial animals. They have evolved alongside the evolution of bioluminescence, rather in the way that colourful flowers and nectar-eating insects have evolved alongside one another on Earth. Eden trees use luminous lanternflowers to attract the creatures that help them reproduce, just as flowering plants on Earth use colour and scent. I gave a lot of thought to the biology of Eden, but I have to admit that, in strictly scientific terms, my imaginary world isn’t entirely viable. Free-floating planets with warm cores? Yes! Not just possible, but a certainty! But free-floating planets with warm surfaces ? Sadly no. More than one astronomer has told me they just couldn’t happen. No matter how many radiator-like trees there might be, I’ve been told, it still wouldn’t be enough to maintain liquid water or a warm atmosphere. Let’s call it “fiction science”, science made up for a story, which works in some places and in others allows itself poetic licence. Almost all science fiction uses fiction science and Dark Eden contains several other examples. I took some liberties with human genetics, for instance. And then there’s the question of how people got to Eden in the first place. (It’s many light years away from Earth.) Like the writers of pretty much all stories set in interstellar space, I pretended that faster-than-light travel was possible and went with that, although it most probably isn’t. (I think that’s OK. It allows us to visit, in our imaginations at least, parts of the universe we could never otherwise hope to reach.) What I wanted from Eden was for it to be a world that hung together well enough to be a satisfying setting for my story, one in which I and my readers could immerse ourselves. item.title: Read an extract from Dark Eden by Chris Beckett
item.description: The New Scientist Book Club is reading Dark Eden by Chris Beckett We went out by a path that led through a big clump of flickering starflowers and then into Batwing. A whole bunch of Batwing grownups and newhairs were in their clearing banging away at a giant redlantern tree with their blackglass axes, working in the pink light of its flowers. We walked round the edge of their clearing to Family Fence, dragged away the branches at the opening, and went out into open forest. No more shelters and campfires ahead of us now: nothing but shining trees. Hmmmph, hmmmph, hmmmph , went the trees. Hmmmmmm , went forest. We walked for a waking under the light of the treelanterns, slashing down whatever birds and bats and fruit we could get as we went along, and finally stopped to rest at the big lump of rock called Lava Blob. Old Roger handed us out a gritty little seedcake each, made of ground-up starflower seeds, so we could have something in our bellies, and then we settled down with our backs against the rock, so we didn’t have to worry about leopards sneaking up behind us. There were lots of yellowlantern trees round there, which we didn’t get so much back in Family, and also yellow animals called hoppers that came bouncing out of forest on their back legs and wrung their four hands together while they looked at us with their big flat eyes and went Peep peep peep . But hoppers were no good to eat and their skins were no use either, so we just chucked stones at them to make them go away and let us sleep in peace. Advertisement Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter When we woke up, Starry Swirl was still bright bright in sky. We ate a bit of dry cake and off we went again, under redlanterns and whitelanterns and spiketrees, with flutterbyes darting and glittering all round us and bats chasing the flutterbyes and trees going hmmph, hmmph, hmmph like always, until it all blurred together into that hmmmmmmmmm that was the background of our lives. After a few miles we came to a small pool full of shiny wavyweed and all us newhairs took off our wraps and dived into the warm water for crabfish and oysters to eat. All the boys watched Tina Spiketree diving in, and they all thought how graceful she was with her long legs, and how smooth her skin was, and how much they wanted to slip with her. But when she came up she swam straight to me, and gave me a dying oyster with the bright pink light still shining out of it. “You know what they say about oysters, don’t you, John?” she said. Tom’s neck, she was pretty pretty, the prettiest in whole of Family. And she knew it well well. In another couple of hours we reached the place where Peckham Hills began to rise up out of forest of Circle Valley, and started to climb up through them by Monkey Path, which isn’t really a path, but just a way we know through the trees. The trees carried on up the slopes – redlanterns and whitelanterns and scalding hot spiketrees – and there were flickering starflowers
item.dc:creator: Chris Beckett
item.content:encoded: The New Scientist Book Club is reading Dark Eden by Chris Beckett We went out by a path that led through a big clump of flickering starflowers and then into Batwing. A whole bunch of Batwing grownups and newhairs were in their clearing banging away at a giant redlantern tree with their blackglass axes, working in the pink light of its flowers. We walked round the edge of their clearing to Family Fence, dragged away the branches at the opening, and went out into open forest. No more shelters and campfires ahead of us now: nothing but shining trees. Hmmmph, hmmmph, hmmmph , went the trees. Hmmmmmm , went forest. We walked for a waking under the light of the treelanterns, slashing down whatever birds and bats and fruit we could get as we went along, and finally stopped to rest at the big lump of rock called Lava Blob. Old Roger handed us out a gritty little seedcake each, made of ground-up starflower seeds, so we could have something in our bellies, and then we settled down with our backs against the rock, so we didn’t have to worry about leopards sneaking up behind us. There were lots of yellowlantern trees round there, which we didn’t get so much back in Family, and also yellow animals called hoppers that came bouncing out of forest on their back legs and wrung their four hands together while they looked at us with their big flat eyes and went Peep peep peep . But hoppers were no good to eat and their skins were no use either, so we just chucked stones at them to make them go away and let us sleep in peace. Advertisement Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter When we woke up, Starry Swirl was still bright bright in sky. We ate a bit of dry cake and off we went again, under redlanterns and whitelanterns and spiketrees, with flutterbyes darting and glittering all round us and bats chasing the flutterbyes and trees going hmmph, hmmph, hmmph like always, until it all blurred together into that hmmmmmmmmm that was the background of our lives. After a few miles we came to a small pool full of shiny wavyweed and all us newhairs took off our wraps and dived into the warm water for crabfish and oysters to eat. All the boys watched Tina Spiketree diving in, and they all thought how graceful she was with her long legs, and how smooth her skin was, and how much they wanted to slip with her. But when she came up she swam straight to me, and gave me a dying oyster with the bright pink light still shining out of it. “You know what they say about oysters, don’t you, John?” she said. Tom’s neck, she was pretty pretty, the prettiest in whole of Family. And she knew it well well. In another couple of hours we reached the place where Peckham Hills began to rise up out of forest of Circle Valley, and started to climb up through them by Monkey Path, which isn’t really a path, but just a way we know through the trees. The trees carried on up the slopes – redlanterns and whitelanterns and scalding hot spiketrees – and there were flickering starflowers growing beneath them, just like in the rest of forest. Streams ran through them down from darkness and ice, heading towards Greatpool, still cold cold but already bright and glittering with life. And small creatures called monkeys jumped from tree to tree. They had little thin bodies, and six long arms with a hand on the end of each. Handsome Fox shot one with an arrow, and was pleased pleased with himself, even though they were all bones and sinews and only give a mouthful of meat, because they move fast and are hard to aim at with those big blotches on their skin that flash on and off as they swing among the lanternflowers. As we climbed up it got colder. The starflowers disappeared, the trees became smaller, and there weren’t any monkeys any more, only the occasional smallbuck darting away through the trees. And then the trees stopped and we came out from the top edge of forest onto bare ground. Pretty soon, when we’d climbed above the height of those last few little trees, we could see whole of Circle Valley spread out below us – whole of Eden that we knew, with thousands and thousands of lanterns shining all the way from where we stood on Peckham Hills to Dark shadow of Blue Mountains away in the distance, and from Rockies over the left, with the red glow of Mount Snellins smouldering in middle, to the deep darkness over to our right that was Alps. And above all of it the huge spiral of Starry Swirl was still shining down. Of course, with no trees to give off light with their lanternflowers or to warm the air with their trunks, it was dark dark up there – you could only just barely make things out in the starlight and the light from the edge of forest – and it was cold cold, specially on our feet. But us newhairs dared each other to run up as far as the snow. The ice felt like it was burning, it was so cold, and most kids took ten twenty steps, yelled and came running down again. But I took Gerry right up to the ridge of the hill and then, ignoring Old Roger yelling at us to come back, went far enough down the other side so that the others couldn’t see us. “We’ve made our point now, haven’t we, John?” Gerry said, shivering. We only had waistwraps on, and buckskins round our shoulders, and our feet were hurting like they’d been skinned. “Shall we go back down to rest of them now?” Read more Our writers pick their favourite science fiction books of all time My cousin Gerry was about a wombtime younger than me – his dad was giving his mum a slip, in other words, about the time that I was born – and he was devoted to me, he thought I was wonderful, he’d do just about anything I asked. “No, wait a minute. Wait a minute. Be quiet and listen.” “Listen to what?” “To the silence, you idiot.” There was no hmmmmmmmm of forest, no hmmph, hmmph, hmmph of pumping trees, no starbirds going hoom, hoom, hoom in the distance, no flutterbyes flapping and flicking, no whoosh of diving bats. There was no sound at all except a quiet little tinkle of water all around us coming out from under the snow in hundreds of little streams. And it was dark dark. No tree-light up there. The only light came from Starry Swirl. We could barely make out each other’s faces. It made me think about that place called Earth where Tommy and Angela first came from, way back in the beginning with the Three Companions, and where one waking we would all return, if only we stayed in the right place and were good good good. There were no lanterntrees back there on Earth, no glittery flutterbyes or shiny flowers, but they had a big big light that we don’t have at all. It came from a giant star. And it was so bright that it would burn out your eyes if you stared at it. “When people talk about Earth,” I said to Gerry, “they always talk about that huge bright star, don’t they, and all the lovely light it must have given? But Earth turned round and round, didn’t it, and half the time it wasn’t facing the star at all but was dark dark, without lanterns or anything, only the light the Earth people made for themselves.” “What are you talking about, John?” Gerry said, with his teeth chattering. “And why can’t we go back down again if you just want to talk?” “I was thinking about that darkness. They called it Night, didn’t they? I’m just thinking that it must have been like this. What you get up here on Snowy Dark: it’s what they would have called Night.” © Chris Beckett This is an extract from Dark Eden by Chris Beckett (Corvus), the November read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here , and join the discussion on Discord here . When you make a purchase via the links on this page, we receive a commission.

item.title: UK Shelly reseller warns payment data stolen after malware found on website
item.description: A UK-based reseller of Shelly smart home equipment has warned customers that their payment data may be compromised after “unauthorized software” was found on its website. “After receiving a warning from our payment provider, Stripe, we investigated and found unauthorized software on our website and server,” the email from Shelly Store UK, seen by The Register , stated. “We removed the identified malicious software, strengthened access security, applied security updates and introduced ongoing monitoring. We have also reported the incident to the Information Commissioner’s Office .” Shelly Store UK informed customers it was unable to determine whether their data was accessed or copied, although all customers who made orders during an unspecified window are being contacted. One punter told us that hours before they received the email from Shelly Store UK, they began a payment dispute with their card provider after a £221.28 transaction, dated October 26, was made in Australia using their details. They suspect their full card details were swiped at some point between October 12, when they made their first and only order with the company, and October 27, when they received the breach notification. Shelly Store UK did not immediately respond to our request for more details. Its notification email stated the internal investigation remains ongoing, and in addition to payment card details, customers may have had their names, billing addresses, and contact details compromised. Shelly Store UK recommended that customers contact their card issuer for guidance on whether they will need a replacement card, and to scour their transaction histories and report any suspicious entries. It also urged caution in receiving communications asking for data such as payment details and security codes, and recommended a password reset . “We’re sorry for the concern and inconvenience this may cause,” the company said. “We are taking this seriously and will contact you if our investigation identifies further information relevant to you.” Shelly Store UK is an authorized reseller of Shelly smart home products and is wholly independent of the main Shelly company. “Shelly Store is a reseller of Shelly and is not part of, owned by, or directly affiliated with Shelly Group,” a Shelly spokesperson said. “We do not manage the Shelly Store website, its business operations, and we do not direct our customers from any of our websites to Shelly Store UK.” ®

item.title: Roster rifts, police raids and Son’s uncertain future leave South Korea at a crossroads
item.description: After a disaster World Cup, the team have continued to spiral, with tensions high between young and older players and the captain’s standing in question Son Heung-min and Cristiano Ronaldo are iconic No 7s, Premier League legends and international record-breakers. Now there is a surprising danger of them having something else in common: being a divisive presence in their national teams. On 21 October, during a parliamentary committee meeting, politician Jeong Yeon-wook put a question to acting Korea Football Association (KFA) president Lee Yong-soo, that took a story out of the sports pages and into the national conversation. “It is said that recently, within the national team squad, players have been calling him not by his name but as ‘No 7’ or ‘that person’. Do you know who that is?” Lee then replied, “Are you referring to Son Heung-min?” Jeong went on: “So it appears to be true. … It has also been revealed that the national team’s leadership is causing discord and has broken down overall.” Lee declined to comment. Continue reading...

item.title: Google's search revenue Ferrari hits an AI-powered speed bump
item.description: Google is paying a higher price for its bet on AI than even Alphabet's $51.4 billion in Q3 capital expenditures suggest. The biz appears to have traded its high-performing search advertising business for the mediocre monetization of AI Overviews and AI Mode, a misstep that contributed to investor concerns as Alphabet lost roughly $500 billion in market value despite management's attempts to reassure Wall Street. Google's year-over-year search revenue growth slowed from 17 percent in Q2 to 12 percent in Q3 . It's still headed in the right direction, but at a slower rate. During Alphabet's conference call for investors, Douglas Anmuth from JPMorgan Chase & Co asked whether that's because Google is showing fewer ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode than it shows in its traditional search results. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler cited several reasons for that: foreign exchange rates, Europe's elimination of its customs-duty exemption, and "the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode." To compensate, Google said it is expanding the distribution of AI Overview ads and adding multiturn ads in the US for AI Mode queries. But some Google Ads customers appear to be more concerned about quality than quantity. In a social media post , Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, complained that Google has responded to declining search volumes by attempting to manufacture revenue growth through "short-sighted, highly extractive, customer-hostile tactics," such as charging advertisers more for lower-quality clicks, including clicks on search terms they had not agreed to target. Eric Seufert, an analyst with Mobile Dev Memo, dismissed the doomsayers in a blog post . "It’s tempting to look at the successive deceleration in Search revenue growth from Q1 2026 as a response to pressure from other chatbots and to assume that Search query volume is migrating elsewhere," he wrote. "But the earnings release notes that the 'year-over-year Search query growth rate [was] the highest it has been in the last five years' in Q3, so it's clear that Search usage isn't declining." So people are still searching, and the business is still growing, but less convincingly, thanks to the lower monetization of AI Overviews and AI Mode. And Google's answer involves more ads in AI interactions. Nate Elliott, principal analyst for AI at Emarketer, told The Register in an email that AI represents a double-edged sword for Google's ad business. "On the one hand, Google owns the thing that people use AI for most: search," Elliott wrote. "Our surveys say that by far the top reason people use AI is to look for facts and information. Luckily for Google, people also tell us they haven't stopped using search engines – they've simply added AI as a new behavior on top of search. That means people spend more time than ever looking for information, and most of those people don't even think twice before doing their searches on Google. item.dc:creator: Thomas Claburn
item.content:encoded: Google is paying a higher price for its bet on AI than even Alphabet's $51.4 billion in Q3 capital expenditures suggest. The biz appears to have traded its high-performing search advertising business for the mediocre monetization of AI Overviews and AI Mode, a misstep that contributed to investor concerns as Alphabet lost roughly $500 billion in market value despite management's attempts to reassure Wall Street. Google's year-over-year search revenue growth slowed from 17 percent in Q2 to 12 percent in Q3 . It's still headed in the right direction, but at a slower rate. During Alphabet's conference call for investors, Douglas Anmuth from JPMorgan Chase & Co asked whether that's because Google is showing fewer ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode than it shows in its traditional search results. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler cited several reasons for that: foreign exchange rates, Europe's elimination of its customs-duty exemption, and "the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode." To compensate, Google said it is expanding the distribution of AI Overview ads and adding multiturn ads in the US for AI Mode queries. But some Google Ads customers appear to be more concerned about quality than quantity. In a social media post , Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, complained that Google has responded to declining search volumes by attempting to manufacture revenue growth through "short-sighted, highly extractive, customer-hostile tactics," such as charging advertisers more for lower-quality clicks, including clicks on search terms they had not agreed to target. Eric Seufert, an analyst with Mobile Dev Memo, dismissed the doomsayers in a blog post . "It’s tempting to look at the successive deceleration in Search revenue growth from Q1 2026 as a response to pressure from other chatbots and to assume that Search query volume is migrating elsewhere," he wrote. "But the earnings release notes that the 'year-over-year Search query growth rate [was] the highest it has been in the last five years' in Q3, so it's clear that Search usage isn't declining." So people are still searching, and the business is still growing, but less convincingly, thanks to the lower monetization of AI Overviews and AI Mode. And Google's answer involves more ads in AI interactions. Nate Elliott, principal analyst for AI at Emarketer, told The Register in an email that AI represents a double-edged sword for Google's ad business. "On the one hand, Google owns the thing that people use AI for most: search," Elliott wrote. "Our surveys say that by far the top reason people use AI is to look for facts and information. Luckily for Google, people also tell us they haven't stopped using search engines – they've simply added AI as a new behavior on top of search. That means people spend more time than ever looking for information, and most of those people don't even think twice before doing their searches on Google. If Google figures out how to effectively monetize those users, that's great news for them." But, said Elliott, people may find tools they like better than Google Search as they become accustomed to AI-based discovery. "If ChatGPT or Claude or Muse is better at helping them find what they're looking for, people's search habits might change for the first time in a generation," he said. "That's potentially catastrophic for Google's ad business. The same is true if they maintain their market share but simply can't figure out how to make money from this new kind of discovery. "The problem is, Google isn't giving us very much information about what the specific impact is of AI on their business right now, so everyone's reading into the tiny scraps of information they are releasing." Elliott said it's remarkable that Google has managed to keep the largest and most mature digital ad business growing at a double-digit rate every quarter in recent years. "But it appears that most folks disagree, and instead are concerned that the advertising business 'only' grew by 10 percent," he said. ®

item.title: The 12 strangest science stories we can’t stop thinking about
item.description: A male Amazon river dolphin ( Inia geoffrensis ) urinating into the air There are some stories that stay with you forever, the big scientific moments that change the course of history. These are not those moments – but we can’t stop thinking about them anyway. Push my button Surgeon Stuart Meloy was performing a pain-relief operation on a woman’s spine when she started exclaiming emphatically. “You’re going to have to teach my husband to do that,” the woman said. This inspired Meloy to invent an implant to help women who are unable to achieve orgasms in the usual way. New Scientist broke the news in 2001, sparking a frenzy of worldwide media excitement. But 13 years later, Meloy was still struggling to raise funds for a full clinical trial, and the “orgasmatron” never reached a climax. Monkey pleasure A long-tailed macaque Shutterstock/fiz_zero We aren’t the only primates capable of coming up with creative ways to pleasure ourselves. In a study of long-tailed macaques ( Macaca fascicularis ) in Bali, Indonesia, Camilla Cenni at the University of Lethbridge in Alberta, Canada, and her colleagues filmed hundreds of examples of male and female monkeys using stone tools as sex toys , rubbing or tapping them on their genitals. According to Cyril Grueter at the University of Western Australia, the Balinese monkeys get plenty of food handouts from humans, and this frees up time for sexual experimentation. But some monkeys in other places have unusual kinks, too: another study reported a wild macaque in Japan rubbing its genitals on the back of a sika deer. Advertisement Head transplants In 2015, surgeon Sergio Canavero announced plans to carry out the first human head transplant, intended to extend the lives of people with muscle and nerve degeneration or widespread cancer. He claimed his technique could overcome technical hurdles, including how to fuse the spinal cord and prevent the body’s immune system from rejecting the head. In the following two years, Canavero published animal experiments supposedly backing up his methods, but other surgeons remained highly sceptical . A human head transplant never did happen, but Canavero has reportedly moved on to an even bolder ambition: transplanting a brain into a non-sentient clone. Rats driving Have you ever wondered if a rat can drive a car? Kelly Lambert at the University of Richmond in Virginia has. She and her colleagues built a tiny car with three copper bars that would steer it left, forward or right. Sure enough, 18 rats learned to drive towards food rewards. They even found it relaxing, as measurements of their stress hormones indicated. item.dc:creator: Sam Wong
item.content:encoded: A male Amazon river dolphin ( Inia geoffrensis ) urinating into the air There are some stories that stay with you forever, the big scientific moments that change the course of history. These are not those moments – but we can’t stop thinking about them anyway. Push my button Surgeon Stuart Meloy was performing a pain-relief operation on a woman’s spine when she started exclaiming emphatically. “You’re going to have to teach my husband to do that,” the woman said. This inspired Meloy to invent an implant to help women who are unable to achieve orgasms in the usual way. New Scientist broke the news in 2001, sparking a frenzy of worldwide media excitement. But 13 years later, Meloy was still struggling to raise funds for a full clinical trial, and the “orgasmatron” never reached a climax. Monkey pleasure A long-tailed macaque Shutterstock/fiz_zero We aren’t the only primates capable of coming up with creative ways to pleasure ourselves. In a study of long-tailed macaques ( Macaca fascicularis ) in Bali, Indonesia, Camilla Cenni at the University of Lethbridge in Alberta, Canada, and her colleagues filmed hundreds of examples of male and female monkeys using stone tools as sex toys , rubbing or tapping them on their genitals. According to Cyril Grueter at the University of Western Australia, the Balinese monkeys get plenty of food handouts from humans, and this frees up time for sexual experimentation. But some monkeys in other places have unusual kinks, too: another study reported a wild macaque in Japan rubbing its genitals on the back of a sika deer. Advertisement Head transplants In 2015, surgeon Sergio Canavero announced plans to carry out the first human head transplant, intended to extend the lives of people with muscle and nerve degeneration or widespread cancer. He claimed his technique could overcome technical hurdles, including how to fuse the spinal cord and prevent the body’s immune system from rejecting the head. In the following two years, Canavero published animal experiments supposedly backing up his methods, but other surgeons remained highly sceptical . A human head transplant never did happen, but Canavero has reportedly moved on to an even bolder ambition: transplanting a brain into a non-sentient clone. Rats driving Have you ever wondered if a rat can drive a car? Kelly Lambert at the University of Richmond in Virginia has. She and her colleagues built a tiny car with three copper bars that would steer it left, forward or right. Sure enough, 18 rats learned to drive towards food rewards. They even found it relaxing, as measurements of their stress hormones indicated. Lambert proposed that driving challenges could replace traditional maze tests when using rat models to study neuropsychiatric conditions. The sniff test Humans are more similar to rats than we like to think. In a psychology experiment, Noam Sobel and his colleagues at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, surreptitiously filmed 153 volunteers. After shaking hands with someone of the same sex, people smelled their shaking hand more than twice as much as they did before the handshake. Puzzlingly, after shaking hands with someone of the opposite sex, people were more likely to sniff their non-shaking hand. The team suspected that humans use chemical signals all the time without being aware of it. Urine fountains Communication through scent is, of course, widespread in mammals, but some never-before-seen behaviour in dolphins took biologists by surprise in 2025. While studying Amazon river dolphins ( Inia geoffrensis ), or botos, in Brazil, Claryana Araújo-Wang at CetAsia Research Group in Ontario, Canada, saw a male “flip his belly up out of the water, expose his penis and then proceed to urinate into the air”, she told New Scientist . They saw dolphins do this a total of 36 times, and most of the time another male was nearby and would pursue the stream of urine. The purpose of this behaviour hasn’t yet been established, but hormones in urine might signal a male’s social position or physical condition, said Araújo-Wang. Read more Orcas have begun wearing salmon hats again – and we may soon know why Giving the finger As for human modes of communication, many of us struggle to put our smartphones down – so the last thing we’d want is for them to crawl across the table towards us. Nevertheless, Marc Teyssier at the University of Paris-Saclay in France and his colleagues gave phones this ability in 2018 , with a robotic appendage dubbed the MobiLimb. It plugs into a device’s USB port and, for some reason, looks eerily like a human finger, giving it a spooky quality reminiscent of Thing from The Addams Family . The MobiLimb can stroke your wrist, wave, wag like a tail or, most disconcertingly, drag the phone around. Thankfully, the idea hasn’t taken off. Horror frog A taxidermied male hairy frog Gustavocarra/CC BY-SA 4.0 If you find the thought of a phone with a finger horrifying, wait until you hear about the nightmare-inducing hairy frog Trichobatrachus robustus. In 2008, researchers reported that these frogs can break their own bones to produce claws that burst through their skin. David Blackburn at Harvard University’s Museum of Comparative Zoology thought these weapons were for defence, but two years later, another team argued that they were used in fights between males – and that the frog’s unusual hairs were a kind of armour to protect its vulnerable parts from sharp claws. Corpse shrinking In 1957, when New Scientist was 1 year old, we reported on a new method for shrinking an adult human body to the size of a baby . At an exhibition of inventors in Winnipeg, Canada, the unnamed inventor of this process claimed it would make disposing of dead bodies simpler, as they could be slid into underground tubes and take up less space. The method involved applying high pressure to the corpse and squeezing out fluids so its flesh could be compressed into a mould. “All this is, of course, highly ingenious but it is uncertain why the inventor thinks that his newly proposed form of burial is in any way better than the current and very popular method of cremation,” the writer mused. Read more The brain has its own microbiome. Here’s what it means for your health Transient anus The warty comb jelly has an anus that comes and goes Andrey Nekrasov/imageBROKER.com​/Alamy We may take it for granted, but the anus, which allows food to pass through the body, was an evolutionary breakthrough, both figuratively and literally. The earliest animals, like jellyfish today, had only one gut opening, where food went in and waste came out. In 2019, scientists discovered that the warty comb jelly ( Mnemiopsis leidyi , pictured top) forms an anal opening when it needs to defecate, but it vanishes straight afterwards. This, they suggested, could represent how the anus evolved in the first place. Fart science Flatus – gas expelled from the anus – has been a topic of endless fascination for many readers (and journalists). In 2001, we featured the work of Michael Levitt at the Veterans Administration Medical Center in Minneapolis, a leading authority on the subject. He developed a “Toot Trapper” that reduces odours by trapping certain gases using activated charcoal. We also reported on a device for monitoring gas emissions from dogs , used to test dog snacks that were supposed to reduce flatulence. In 2016, researchers in Australia worked out which foods cause the smelliest farts by mixing faeces with different foods. They recommended eating less protein and more slow-release carbohydrates to minimise hydrogen sulphide production. In 2022, Nagarajan Kannan at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, and his colleagues worked out that some poos float because of gas from gut microbes , confirming a hypothesis first put forward by Levitt 50 years earlier. item.title: Farm PC 'maintained' by a 14-year-old dumped support chap in a steaming pile of tech mess
item.description: Welcome to another instalment of On Call, the reader-contributed column The Register publishes each Friday as a cathartic service for readers who know that dealing with tech support BS can be a cow of a job. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Jason" who told us he had helped an agricultural equipment dealer with his computer issues for about 20 years. "One day this guy called me to ask if I could help at a farm in Yorkshire, where he'd arranged the supply and installation of a fairly substantial system that used a computer to do effectively everything for a few hundred cattle," he told On Call. "That meant individually feeding them, measuring milk yields, planning pregnancies, and periodically submitting all the data to the government." Jason said other tech support folk had tried, and failed, to fix the system. "This had somewhat soured the relationship between the agricultural equipment dealer and the farmer," he punned in his email to On Call. Well punned, Jason. But we digress. "Despite not being fond of wading around in cow shit at four in the morning, I agreed to take a look at the system," Jason told us. By this time he had learned that the farm produced many tons of milk each week, so assumed he would find serious industrial-scale tech once he reached the farm. That assumption was wrong. "When I arrived, the first thing that I found to worry about was that the whole thing was controlled by proprietary software on a single PC running Windows XP – just after Microsoft ended mainstream support." The other things to worry about were all acts of omission: the farm had no backups, no spare PC, and nobody on site to maintain the PC. Jason asked if anyone was responsible for keeping the computer up to date with the security patches and was told the farmer's 14-year-old grandson had done some computer studies at school, so he got the job. That lad had either not discovered, or deleted, the many rather racy videos Jason found on the PC. "When the farmer's wife learned of this, there was what can best be described as a hullabaloo," Jason told On Call. As he dug into the mess, Jason found that the computer was sending milk production data to Her Majesty's Government. He also found that neither the government, nor the farm management software vendor, had bothered to require installation of a firewall. Jason says he installed one, made a few other tweaks, and got the system working. "Everyone seemed pleased, or at least they did until they got my bill," he wrote. "And to be fair, they did pay it promptly." Jason never heard from the farm again. "I don't know if that's because it's still working OK, or if they're just too embarrassed to see me again, or they found someone cheaper who could cope with my recommendations," he wrote. What's the strangest or dirtiest place you've been asked to deliver tech support? Don't cheese us off by holding back! Click here to send us your story so we can milk it for all it's worth in a future instalment of On

item.title: AWS installs an AI accelerator every 14 seconds and eyes $1 trillion annual revenue
item.description: Amazon Web Services will become a trillion-dollar business in five to ten years, and thanks to the AI boom Amazon CEO Andy Jassy thinks it should be able to grow by 40 percent or more in 2027 or 2028. The cloud giant is already on track to generate $184 billion annual revenue this financial year, helped by 39.3 percent year-over-year growth that propelled Q3 revenue to a whisker short of $46 billion. “It’s important to remember that the vast majority of global IT spend, about 85 percent, is still on premises, and we’re in a 10- to 20-year cycle where that equation will flip to the cloud,” he said on Amazon's Q3 earnings call. “Conventional wisdom has been that linchpin workloads like mainframes or storage area networks would never move to the cloud,” he observed, before triumphantly noting “these workloads are moving.” He thinks AI will help, too. Jassy said the cloudy concern installs a new AI accelerator “about every 14 seconds, and almost as fast as we install capacity, customers are gobbling it up.” The outfit’s Bedrock AI services is already the fastest growing multi-billion dollar service in its history, Jassy said. Core compute and storage services are also soaring: the CEO said revenue from both “grew at their fastest rates in several years.” Jassy thinks the performance of Bedrock and core services are intertwined, because when users select AWS for AI workloads they want their cloudy inferencing rigs to be “near the rest of their data and apps.” The CEO said AI workloads therefore “can’t help but drive core AWS demand because AI uses core for work like reinforcement learning, post-training, and tool usage, which can’t help but drive reinvestment back into our broader AWS functionality.” He thinks this scheme is already working because margins for AI services are already “well ahead” of the figures AWS was able to achieve for its core services at a similar time in their evolution. The company expects to make $220 billion of capital expenditure in 2026 and already spent $75.9 billion last quarter alone, most of that on AWS. Jassy said the cloud colossus is finding ways to more quickly pay for its infrastructure investments. The CEO said it’s not easy to do that. “I think what we’re seeing with AI, it’s the biggest transformation in our lifetime,” he said. “Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years? Yeah, it might be more convenient, but that’s not the world that we live in, and that’s not the opportunity.” “We can fund this plan. I think it will forever change the size of Amazon. It will forever change our revenue, it will forever change our free cash flow, and we’re going to invest, and we’re going to pursue it to continue to be the significant leader like we are today.” Amazon needs AWS to land this plane, because the cloudy concern is growing much faster than the company’s retail and operations, which saw revenue rise six percent on far sl

Yeah, it might be more convenient, but that’s not the world that we live in, and that’s not the opportunity.” “We can fund this plan. I think it will forever change the size of Amazon. It will forever change our revenue, it will forever change our free cash flow, and we’re going to invest, and we’re going to pursue it to continue to be the significant leader like we are today.” Amazon needs AWS to land this plane, because the cloudy concern is growing much faster than the company’s retail and operations, which saw revenue rise six percent on far slimmer margins. Jassy could at least point to Prime Video becoming “a significant business with a revenue run rate in the tens of billions of dollars, [and is] now profitable in its own right.” Overall revenue was $180.17 bilion for the quarter. So if the respective growth rates of AWS and the rest of Amazon continue, in a few years we could be talking about a cloud company with a retail side hustle. ®

item.title: Electrocutions, disease and no pay: how workers risk exploitation in Europe’s datacentres
item.description: As thousands of datacentres are constructed across Europe, the Guardian and Investigate Europe have uncovered disturbing evidence that some workers building them are exposed to dangerous conditions and living in fear of speaking out Sandu* checked his watch. He was winding down the last 15 minutes of his shift at a vast Google datacentre site in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium, in March, when the call came in. The 34-year-old electrical tester had already worked almost 10 hours, but says such last-minute jobs were normal: “I had no choice. People have been fired after saying no.” The task was one Sandu had done many times before and involved a series of tests measuring the safety and integrity of the electrical wiring. A protective suit was locked away in an equipment room. The round trip would have added another 15 minutes to the job, he says, and people were waiting, so he decided not to retrieve the suit. Continue reading...

item.title: In the year AI re-wrote the infosec rulebook, it’s comforting to know crypto exchanges still have bad security
item.description: Crypto exchange Binance has paused trading after discovering unknown parties cracked one of its workers’ laptops and used it to make massive trades. Late on Thursday, US time, the company used its social media feeds to report “Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.” The exchange insisted “User funds are completely safe” and warned its customers “should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.” The company soon froze $2.5 billion worth of assets and warned that the figure could go higher “as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.” To prevent the matter worsening, Binance halted all trading, deposits, and withdrawals. It also promised to cover any losses. About an hour ago at the time of writing, Binance posted an update on the incident that explains what it thinks went wrong. “Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions,” the post states. The company also hiked the amount it thinks is at risk to $6.3 billion and repeated its promise to cover any customer losses. The update also says Binance found no evidence of any wallet private key leak, suggesting that customers’ holdings remain secure. When they can use them again, as Binance is yet to resume trading. Binance hasn’t explained how attackers gained access to the engineer’s laptop. The scant details provided make it hard to rule out a successful phishing attack, or perhaps a supply chain attack on a package the developer used. Binance says it will spill once it knows exactly what happened. Cryptocurrency outfits have a long and inglorious history of falling victim to cyberattacks, perhaps starting with the 2011 raid on Mt Gox , to incidents allegedly perpetrated by nation-states , and, just last week, another situation possibly involving an AI-powered attacker . ®

item.title: APOD: 2026 October 30 – Haunting the Cepheus Flare
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 October 30 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Haunting the Cepheus Flare Explanation: Spooky shapes seem to haunt this dusty expanse, drifting through the night in the royal constellation Cepheus . Of course, the shapes are cosmic dust clouds visible in dimly reflected starlight. Far from your own neighborhood , they lurk above the plane of the Milky Way at the edge of the Cepheus Flare molecular cloud complex some 1,200 light-years away. Over 2 light-years across and brighter than most of the other ghostly apparitions, vdB 141 or Sh2-136 is also known as the Ghost Nebula . It lies at lower right in the starry field of view. Inside the Ghost Nebula are reddish telltale signs of dense cores collapsing in the early stages of star formation . With the eerie hue of interstellar dust reflecting bluish light from hot young stars of NGC 7023, the Iris Nebula stands out against the dark just left of center. In the broad telescopic frame , these fertile interstellar dust fields stretch almost six full moons across the sky. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin Part of an ice-covered Antarctic island has the appearance of a grinning skull in profile. Some of the face has a gray appearance where seasonal snow is gone and bare ice is exposed. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin March 22, 2025 October 10, 2026 Part of an ice-covered Antarctic island has the appearance of a grinning skull in profile, with a rock outcrop as an eye socket and lateral moraine as a mouth. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin Part of an ice-covered Antarctic island has the appearance of a grinning skull in profile. Some of the face has a gray appearance where seasonal snow is gone and bare ice is exposed. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin March 22, 2025 October 10, 2026 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Shrouded in ice in the lonely Weddell Sea, Vega Island is an eerie sight to behold. On this speck of land east of the Antarctic Peninsula, ice, rock outcrops, and glacial moraines combine to create the appearance of a smirking skull in profile looking toward Devil Island. These images show Vega Island’s creepy countenance at the start of austral autumn (left) and in spring (right). They were acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.) A nunatak jutting out of the ice has the appearance of an eye socket, a lateral moraine forms a mouth, and Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier constitutes a jawbone. In the March 2025 image, a layer of snow coats the ice, which is typical of the region’s wettest month. That contrasts with the October 2026 image, when snow is absent from large areas and darker ice surfaces are visible. Above-average temperatures in winter 2026 —particularly in June —were partly responsible for so much bare ice in October , said glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College. The ice exposed on Vega and nearby islands indicates limited new snow accumulation over the winter, further reduced by sublimation and wind scouring, he said. “The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.” The melt season ahead may also be more trick than treat. Bare ice is darker than snow and absorbs more solar energy, meaning that melting is poised to speed up as the days grow longer and warmer. “Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” Pelto said. “When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.” October 10, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin The first comprehensive mapping of Vega Island’s ice was aided by Landsat imagery. In a study published in 1982 , scientists described the island’s four ice caps with protruding rocky cliffs and outlet glaciers. They leveraged early Landsat observations along with aerial photos and topographic maps to catalog 29 glaciers on Vega. Of those glaciers, Devil’s Bay Glacier has been closely monitored since the austral summer of 1998-1999, with researchers measuring an overall decline in its mass. Satellite images acquired in recent decades show ice loss from other glaciers on the island as well, with increased areas of exposed bedrock. Long before scientists began tracking its glaciers, Vega was a bright spot in a tale of terror born out of early exploration of the area. The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901-1903 set out to study the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife on and around the eastern Antarctic Peninsula. The party became split into three groups during their explorations, isolated for a winter in different locations. Adding to the horror, they lost their ship to the pack ice. Cape Well-met, as it would come to be known, off the “forehead” of the Vega Island skull, was the site of a happy reunion of two of the groups in spring 1903. Soon thereafter, an Argentinean expedition rescued the survivors of the ordeal. NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . item.title: Can We Talk About Tenicka Boyd’s Lagos Fashion Week Style?
item.description: The American fashion influencer, whose effortlessly polished approach to dressing has earned her a devoted following, has been turning heads in Lagos with a wardrobe that’s equal parts playful and unapologetically sophisticated. And if there’s one thing her appearances have made clear, it’s that Boyd understands the assignment when it comes to fashion week. Scroll through Tenicka Boyd’s standout Lagos Fashion Week looks below. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram For her Jewel Jemila appearance, Boyd embraced full-on romance in a sweeping fuchsia dress, complete with cascading ruffles and dramatic bell sleeves. Paired with gold jewellery and her signature sleek, centre-parted hair, the look was a masterclass in polished style. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram She switched gears for Beverly Naya ’s Skin Summit experience, opting for a striking black-and-white body-skimming dress with an abstract, zebra-inspired pattern and dramatic fringe detailing. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram But perhaps her most playful look came courtesy of The LadyMaker . Tenicka Boyd/Instagram Boyd paired a sculptural hot-pink puff-sleeve top with a voluminous orange bubble skirt, finishing the look with a purple tasseled handbag and coordinating heels. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram And then there’s this insanely detailed Onalaja burgundy beaded ensemble, a rich, intricately embellished look that traded playful volume for texture and craftsmanship, reinforcing Boyd’s ability to move between different fashion moods without losing her distinct point of view. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Tenicka (@tenickab) Beyond the clothes, Boyd’s Lagos emphasizes the growing visibility of African designers on the global fashion stage. For an influencer whose wardrobe regularly spans international luxury houses and emerging labels, we love that her enthusiasm for Nigerian fashion feels like a natural extension of her personal style. And with looks this good, we’re definitely paying attention. Photography: Ayo Makinwa The post Can We Talk About Tenicka Boyd’s Lagos Fashion Week Style? appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: PC chip plunge wipes out a quarter of Intel’s value
item.description: Intel’s share price sank by almost a quarter on Thursday after the company revealed a deep dip in sales of PC processors. The rout began after the silicon-slinger posted Q3 results that included some nice numbers, such as a 21 percent year on year revenue jump to $16.5 billion, helped by 78 percent growth for datacenter and AI products, and gross margins of 43 percent. The revenue number was at the high end of Intel’s revenue guidance of $15.8-16.8 billion, and the gross margin beat its predictions by two points. Outweighing those upsides was a decline in revenue for client computing and physical AI products, which saw incoming cash reach $8.1 billion but fall five percent year-over-year and nine percent decline from last quarter. In prepared remarks [PDF] published to coincide with Intel’s earnings announcement, CEO Lip Bu Tan said “In recent weeks, our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on memory prices and availability. Year-to-date system end-point prices have increased significantly placing additional pressure on already limited IT budgets.” “The pace of the PC correction has accelerated over the last two months, as our OEM partners are aggressively managing inventory to match the softer sell through,” he added, before predicting that the market for PC chips will shrink by 12 percent next year and remain tough “until memory availability and prices begin to normalize.” Which may not be for years, given Korean memory-maker SK Hynix this week predicted that memory shortages will persist until the year 2030. Intel’s biggest business is therefore in trouble. AI and Xeons riding to a rocky rescue Tan tried to give investors reasons to be cheerful, by saying Intel sees a “resurgence in demand for CPU” sparked by customers’ desire for computing systems that consume less energy. “Increasingly, energy efficiency is becoming the most important metric for the AI infrastructure build-out,” he said. That matters, Tan argued, because “While GPUs are great at ‘thinking tasks,’ deterministic CPUs are far more efficient at ‘finding’ tasks. While a GPU reasoning query can run as high as multiple watt-hours of energy, a single CPU-based query could cost only joules of energy.” The CEO reasoned that lower energy consumption is important in the context of agentic AI – the idea that we will all soon run many autonomous agents to handle personal and professional scutwork. “Applying even conservative estimates to the total number of digital agents, and agents serviced per CPU, it is easy to anticipate a massive dollar and unit TAM [total addressable market] for CPUs over the coming five years,” Tan said. “By our estimates, server CPU TAM, largely driven by agentic workloads, could increase as much as 5X from where it is today, from $40B to more than $200B over five years.” But during its earnings call, Intel execs admitted it may struggle to cash in on that boom in the short and longer term as the company struggles to source key supplies like silicon wafe

Year-to-date system end-point prices have increased significantly placing additional pressure on already limited IT budgets.” “The pace of the PC correction has accelerated over the last two months, as our OEM partners are aggressively managing inventory to match the softer sell through,” he added, before predicting that the market for PC chips will shrink by 12 percent next year and remain tough “until memory availability and prices begin to normalize.” Which may not be for years, given Korean memory-maker SK Hynix this week predicted that memory shortages will persist until the year 2030. Intel’s biggest business is therefore in trouble. AI and Xeons riding to a rocky rescue Tan tried to give investors reasons to be cheerful, by saying Intel sees a “resurgence in demand for CPU” sparked by customers’ desire for computing systems that consume less energy. “Increasingly, energy efficiency is becoming the most important metric for the AI infrastructure build-out,” he said. That matters, Tan argued, because “While GPUs are great at ‘thinking tasks,’ deterministic CPUs are far more efficient at ‘finding’ tasks. While a GPU reasoning query can run as high as multiple watt-hours of energy, a single CPU-based query could cost only joules of energy.” The CEO reasoned that lower energy consumption is important in the context of agentic AI – the idea that we will all soon run many autonomous agents to handle personal and professional scutwork. “Applying even conservative estimates to the total number of digital agents, and agents serviced per CPU, it is easy to anticipate a massive dollar and unit TAM [total addressable market] for CPUs over the coming five years,” Tan said. “By our estimates, server CPU TAM, largely driven by agentic workloads, could increase as much as 5X from where it is today, from $40B to more than $200B over five years.” But during its earnings call, Intel execs admitted it may struggle to cash in on that boom in the short and longer term as the company struggles to source key supplies like silicon wafers. Asked if Intel can meet demand for server CPUs and if investors should therefore expect further growth in datacenter product sales early in Intel’s next financial year, chief financial officer Dave Zinsner declined to offer any guidance. “There is going to be a strong driver of demand for CPUs,” he demurred. “We see that continuing all through next year. We are working on the supply side of the equation to make sure that we can meet what customers need. We will likely not fully meet what they require, but I think we are going to be in a more challenging situation in the first half of the year than we are in the second half.” Intel is trying to shift production around its fleet of fabs so it can crank out as much silicon as possible and will even devote some PC chip production capacity to datacenter products. But overall, Chipzilla is clearly in a spot of bother. CEO Lip Bu Tan said his plan to “rebuild” Intel will be “a multiyear journey” and insisted “We have made enormous strides in these 18 months, including a dramatic re-sizing of our workforce, eliminating middle management and bureaucracy, streamlining our executive ranks and establishing an almost entirely new leadership team.” He pointed to strong progress on Intel’s manufacturing processes that will bring it closer to parity with TSMC, meaning its own products will become more potent while the company’s foundry business also becomes more attractive. And he said that Intel has restored an “engineering-centric culture” that will help the company to improve. But the CEO also admitted “I am disappointed that we were not able to meet strong customer demand in this quarter.” “We face near term challenges, including manufacturing supply shortages, the unprecedented memory crunch, and the resulting softness in PC demand. But I remain confident in our path forward.” Investors did not share that confidence. Intel’s shares started the day at $92.96 apiece. Immediately after the company announced its results, shares sank to $73. At the time of writing, after-hours trading has seen the price reach $70.87, a 23.7 percent slump. ®

item.title: Map Showing Potential Origins of Martian Meteorite Teghaza 001
item.description: 1 Min Read Map Showing Potential Origins of Martian Meteorite Teghaza 001 PIA26802 Credits: NASA/JPL-Caltech/USGS Photojournal Navigation Science Photojournal Map Showing Potential Origins… Photojournal Home Photojournal Search Latest Content Galleries Feedback RSS About Downloads Map Showing Potential Origins of Martian Meteorite Teghaza 001 JPEG (1.22 MB) Description This global map of Mars shows 13 locations that match the mineralogy and chemistry of Teghaza 001, one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth. While scientists can never know for sure where a Martian meteorite originated, Teghaza 001 includes clues that link it to highlands in the southern hemisphere of the Red Planet. The base map of this image was produced with data from the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter instrument aboard NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor mission. Scientists used data from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter to identify areas of the map (noted with white circles) that have similar mineralogy and chemistry as Teghaza 001. item.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
item.description: Bruno Fernandes owes Manchester United a performance, Mathys Tel has arrived at Spurs and Liverpool are improving Premier League top scorers Michael Carrick and Bruno Fernandes held clear-the-air talks this week. Fernandes was an unused substitute against Bournemouth after criticising Carrick’s tactics during the Champions League defeat at Como but it seems the situation has been resolved – for now. Dropping Fernandes did not do United any good against Bournemouth, who ran riot at Old Trafford , and the captain is expected to return to the starting lineup for the trip to Chelsea.
